params.question: Which of the following best explains why antihistamines used for allergic rhinitis must target H1 receptors rather than H2 receptors?

answers.text: H2 receptors are found only in the brain and do not mediate peripheral allergic responses

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: H2 receptors are found peripherally, predominantly on gastric parietal cells, not in the brain. They regulate acid secretion rather than allergic symptoms.

answers.text: H1 receptors mediate the allergic symptoms (sneezing, itching, rhinorrhoea), while H2 receptors regulate gastric acid secretion

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Histamine acting on H1 receptors produces the cardinal allergy symptoms — sneezing via the trigeminal nerve, rhinorrhoea via vasodilation, itching via sensory nerve stimulation, and congestion via vascular engorgement. H2 receptors sit on parietal cells and control acid output, so blocking them treats peptic disease, not allergy.

answers.text: H2 receptors are activated only during the late-phase allergic response, four to eight hours later

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The late-phase response is driven by newly synthesised inflammatory mediators such as leukotrienes and cytokines, not by H2 receptor activation.

answers.text: Blocking H2 receptors would worsen nasal congestion by increasing blood vessel dilation

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: H2 blockers do not affect nasal vascular tone. They reduce gastric acid secretion and have no role in nasal mucosal blood flow regulation.

overallFeedback.feedback: Review the distinction: H1 receptors in the nose, eyes, and skin drive allergy symptoms (sneezing, itching, rhinorrhoea, congestion). H2 receptors on gastric parietal cells control acid secretion. Only H1 blockers treat allergic rhinitis.
Exactly right. H1 receptors mediate all the hallmark symptoms of allergic rhinitis, making H1 antagonists the logical therapeutic target. H2 receptors are irrelevant to nasal allergy.

metadata.title: Which of the following best explains why

interactions.label: A 62-year-old man with hypertension and moderate persistent allergic rhinitis re

params.question: A 62-year-old man with hypertension and moderate persistent allergic rhinitis requests a nasal decongestant spray for quick relief of congestion. What is the most appropriate advice?

answers.text: Recommend oral pseudoephedrine as the first-line agent for his nasal congestion

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Oral pseudoephedrine is a sympathomimetic and must be avoided in patients with hypertension, hyperthyroidism, or ischaemic heart disease due to its cardiovascular effects.

answers.text: Prescribe oxymetazoline nasal spray for regular daily use throughout the allergy season

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Oxymetazoline gives rapid relief but must be limited to 3–5 days. Prolonged use causes rhinitis medicamentosa (rebound congestion), worsening the very symptom it was meant to treat.

answers.text: Start an intranasal corticosteroid as the primary treatment and limit any decongestant spray to three to five days

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: For moderate-to-severe persistent allergic rhinitis, intranasal corticosteroids (fluticasone, mometasone, budesonide) are the most effective single agents, targeting both early and late-phase inflammation. Any decongestant spray should be restricted to 3–5 days to prevent rebound congestion.

answers.text: Switch to a first-generation antihistamine for its stronger drying effect on nasal secretions

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: First-generation antihistamines cause sedation and anticholinergic effects. They should be avoided in elderly patients because of the increased risk of falls, cognitive impairment, and urinary retention.

overallFeedback.feedback: For moderate-to-severe persistent allergic rhinitis, intranasal corticosteroids are the most effective single agents. Decongestant sprays must be limited to 3–5 days (rebound risk), pseudoephedrine is contraindicated in hypertension, and first-generation antihistamines are unsafe in elderly patients.

Well done. Intranasal corticosteroids are first-line for moderate-to-severe allergic rhinitis. Decongestant sprays are adjuncts only, limited to 3–5 days. Both pseudoephedrine and first-generation antihistamines are inappropriate in this patient.

interactions.label: Aspirin's antiplatelet effect wears off within 24 hours of the last dose because

params.question: Aspirin's antiplatelet effect wears off within 24 hours of the last dose because its plasma half-life is only 15 to 20 minutes.

l10n.wrongAnswerMessage: Aspirin does have a short half-life of 15–20 minutes, but its mechanism is irreversible covalent acetylation of platelet COX-1. Platelets have no nucleus, so they cannot produce new COX enzyme. The antiplatelet effect therefore lasts the full platelet lifespan of 7–10 days — far longer than 24 hours. Every other NSAID acts reversibly, which is why only aspirin has this uniquely prolonged antiplatelet action.
l10n.correctAnswerMessage: Correct — the statement is false. Although aspirin's half-life is short, it irreversibly acetylates a serine residue on platelet COX-1. Since platelets lack nuclei and cannot synthesise new enzyme, the antiplatelet effect persists for the platelet's entire lifespan of 7–10 days. This is exactly why aspirin must be stopped well before elective surgery.

params.question: Which of the following best explains why an acute gout attack produces a more intense inflammatory response than osteoarthritis?

answers.text: Gout involves autoantibody-driven destruction of the synovial membrane, recruiting immune complexes that erode cartilage, unlike the non-immune process in osteoarthritis

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Autoantibody-mediated synovial destruction with pannus formation describes rheumatoid arthritis, not gout. Gout is a crystal deposition disease driven by innate immunity, not adaptive autoimmunity.

answers.text: Gout preferentially affects large weight-bearing joints with abundant synovial fluid, producing more intense mechanical irritation than the small-joint pattern of osteoarthritis

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Gout classically targets the first metatarsophalangeal joint (podagra), a small joint. The intensity of inflammation is driven by crystal-induced immune activation, not joint size or mechanical factors.

answers.text: Monosodium urate crystals activate the NLRP3 inflammasome, triggering IL-1β release and neutrophil recruitment, whereas osteoarthritis is primarily a mechanical degenerative process

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: MSU crystals activate the NLRP3 inflammasome in synovial macrophages, releasing IL-1β and recruiting neutrophils. Frustrated phagocytosis by these neutrophils releases lysosomal enzymes and reactive oxygen species, intensifying inflammation. Osteoarthritis, by contrast, is driven by mechanical cartilage breakdown with only minor secondary inflammation.

answers.text: Osteoarthritis is driven by CGRP-mediated neurovascular events in the joint capsule, producing a less intense response than the immune-complex deposition seen in gout

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: CGRP-mediated neurovascular events describe the mechanism of migraine, not osteoarthritis. OA is a degenerative condition driven by mechanical wear and progressive cartilage loss.

overallFeedback.feedback: In gout, MSU crystals activate the NLRP3 inflammasome in macrophages → IL-1β release → neutrophil influx → frustrated phagocytosis → intense inflammation. Osteoarthritis is primarily mechanical cartilage degeneration with minimal immune activation. Do not confuse gout with RA (autoimmune pannus) or OA with migraine (CGRP-mediated neurovascular).

Exactly right. Gout's intense inflammation stems from crystal-driven NLRP3 inflammasome activation and neutrophil-mediated frustrated phagocytosis — a fundamentally different mechanism from the mechanical wear of osteoarthritis.

metadata.title: Which of the following best explains why

interactions.label: A 55-year-old woman with recurrent gout attacks is started on low-dose aspirin f

params.question: A 55-year-old woman with recurrent gout attacks is started on low-dose aspirin for cardiovascular prophylaxis. Which of the following is the most likely effect of aspirin on her gout?

answers.text: It will reduce acute gout attacks by inhibiting COX-2-mediated inflammation in the joints

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: At low cardiovascular doses, aspirin's anti-inflammatory effect is negligible and does not prevent gout attacks. Its impact on uric acid handling is the clinically relevant concern in this patient.

answers.text: It will lower serum uric acid by acting as a uricosuric agent at low doses

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Aspirin is uricosuric only at very high doses (above 3 g/day). At low cardiovascular doses, it has the opposite effect — it retains urate by inhibiting tubular secretion.

answers.text: It will prevent urate crystal deposition by blocking the NLRP3 inflammasome

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Aspirin does not act on the NLRP3 inflammasome. Drugs like colchicine interfere with the crystal-induced inflammatory cascade. Aspirin's problem in gout is metabolic, not immunological.

answers.text: It will worsen hyperuricaemia by reducing renal urate excretion

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: At low doses, aspirin inhibits renal tubular urate secretion, reducing urate excretion and raising serum uric acid levels. This can precipitate gout flares, which is precisely why the video emphasises that aspirin has no place in gout management.

overallFeedback.feedback: Low-dose aspirin reduces renal urate excretion, worsening hyperuricaemia and potentially precipitating gout attacks. It is explicitly avoided in gout management. Remember: matching the wrong drug to the wrong condition or phase can cause harm rather than relief.

Well done. Low-dose aspirin worsens hyperuricaemia by inhibiting renal urate excretion — a critical drug-disease interaction to recognise when managing a patient with both cardiovascular risk and gout.
